edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De monogamia, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Post vetera exempla originalium personarum, aeque ad vetera transeamus instrumenta legalium Scripturarum, ut per ordinem de omni nostra paratura retractemus. Et quoniam quidam interdum nihil sibi dicunt esse cum lege, quam Christus non dissolvit, sed adimplevit, interdum quae volunt legis arripiunt; plane et nos sic dicimus decessisse legem, ut onera quidem ejus, quae secundum sententiam Apostolorum nec Patres sustinere voluerunt, concesserint; quae vero ad justitiam spectant, non tantum reservata permaneant, verum et ampliata: ut scilicet redundare possit justitia nostra super Scribarum et Pharisaeorum justitiam. Si justitio, utique et pudicitia. Si ergo, quoniam in lege praecipitur, ut quis fratris sui uxorem sine liberis defuncti in matrimonium adsumat, ad suscitandum fratri suo semen, idque saepius evenire in unam personam potest secundum callidam illam quaestionem Sadducaeorum, ideo et alias putant permissam frequentiam nuptiarum; intelligere debebunt primo rationem ipsius praecepti, et ita scient illam rationem jam cessantem ex eis esse quae evacuata sunt legis. Necessario succedendum erat in matrimonium fratris sine liberis defuncti. Primum, quia adhuc vetus illa benedictio decurrere habebat: Crescite et redundate. Dehinc, quoniam patrum delicta etiam de filiis exigebantur. Tertio, quoniam spadones et steriles ignominiosi habebantur. Itaque, ne proinde maledicti judicarentur, qui non naturae reatu, at mortis praeventu orbi decessissent, ideo illis ex suo genere vicaria, et quasi postuma soboles supparabatur. At ubi et Crescite et redundate evacuavit extremitas temporum, inducente Apostolo: Superest, ut et qui habent uxores, sic sint, ac si non habeant, quia tempus in collecto est; et: Desiit uva acerba, a patribus manducata, fitiorum dentes obstupefacere: unusquisque enim in suo delicto morietur; et spadones non tantum ignominia caruerunt, verum et gratiam meruerunt, invitati in regna coelorum, sepulta lege succedendi in matrimonium fratris, contrarium ejus obtinuit non succedendi in matrimonium fratris. Et ita, ut praediximus, quod cessavit valere, cessante ratione, non potest alii argumentationem accommodare. Ergo non nubet defuncto viro uxor, fratri utique nuptura si nupserit. Omnes enim nos fratres sumus: et illa nuptura in Domino habet nubere, id est, non ethnico, sed fratri; quia et vetus lex adimit conjugium allophylorum. Cum autem et in Levitico cautum sit: Quicumque sumpserit fratris uxorem, immunditia est, turpitudo, sine liberis morietur; sine dubio, dum ille prohibetur denuo nubere, et illa prohibetur, non habens nubere nisi fratri. Quomodo ergo Apostolo conveniet et Legi, quam non in totum impugnat, cum ad epistolam ipsius venerimus, ostendetur. Interim quod pertineat ad Legem, magis nobis competunt argumentationes ejus. Denique prohibet eadem, sacerdotes denuo nubere. Filiam quoque sacerdotis jubet viduam vel ejectam, si semen non fuerit illi, in domum patris sui regredi, et de pane ejus ali. Ideo, si semen non fuerit illi, non, ut si fuerit, denuo nubat: quanto magis enim non nubet, si filios habeat! sed ut, si habuerit, a filio potius alatur quam a patre, quo et filius praeceptum Dei exsequatur, Honora patrem et matrem. Nos autem Jesus summus sacerdos et magnus Patris, de suo vestiens, sacerdotes Deo Patri suo fecit secundum Joannem. Nam et illum adolescentem festinantem ad exequias patris ideo revocat, ut ostendat sacerdotes nos vocari ab eo, quos lex vetabat parentum sepulturae adesse: Super omnem, inquit, animam defunctam sacerdos non introibit, et super patrem suum, et super matrem suam non contaminabitur. Ergo et nos hoc interdictum observare debemus? non utique. Vivit enim unicus pater noster Deus, et mater Ecclesia; et neque ipsi mortui sumus, qui Deo vivimus; neque mortuos sepelimus, quia et illi vivunt in Christo. Certe sacerdotes sumus a Christo vocati, monogamiae debitores ex pristina Dei lege, quae nos tunc in suis sacerdotibus prophetavit.
pass_a_gloss: After the old examples of original persons, let us also pass on to the old instruments of legal Scriptures, so that in order we may reconsider our entire preparation. And since some people sometimes say that they have nothing to do with the law, which Christ did not dissolve, but fulfilled, sometimes they seize what they want of the law; plainly we also say that the law has passed away, so that its burdens, which according to the opinion of the Apostles even the Fathers did not want to bear, have been conceded; but those things which pertain to justice, not only remain reserved, but also have been expanded: so that our justice may abound over the justice of the Scribes and Pharisees. If justice, then also chastity. If, therefore, because it is commanded in the law that someone should take his brother's wife, who has died without children, into marriage, to raise up seed for his brother, and this can often happen to one person according to that cunning question of the Sadducees, therefore they also think that frequency of marriages is permitted; they ought to understand first the reason of that command, and thus they will know that that reason has already ceased to be among the things that have been evacuated of the law. It was necessary to succeed into marriage of a brother who had died without children. First, because that old blessing still had to run its course: Be fruitful and multiply. Next, because the sins of the fathers were also exacted from the children. Third, because eunuchs and sterile people were considered ignominious. And so, lest they be judged accursed, who had not died by nature's debt, but by death's prevention, therefore for them a vicarious and, as it were, posthumous offspring was provided from their own kind. But when both Be fruitful and multiply and the extremity of times have evacuated, the Apostle introducing: It remains that even those who have wives should be as if they did not have them, because the time is short; and: The sour grape, which the fathers ate, will set the children's teeth on edge: for each one will die in his own sin; and eunuchs not only did not suffer ignominy, but also merited grace, invited into the kingdoms of heaven, the law of succeeding into marriage of a brother having been buried, the contrary of not succeeding into marriage of a brother obtained. And so, as we have said before, what has ceased to be valid, with the reason having ceased, cannot accommodate another argument. Therefore, the wife of a deceased husband will not marry, certainly not to the brother if she marries. For we are all brothers: and that marriage in the Lord has to marry, that is, not to an ethnic person, but to a brother; because even the old law takes away marriage to those who are not of the same kind. But when also in Leviticus it has been cautioned: Whoever takes his brother's wife, it is an impurity, a shame, he will die without children; without doubt, while he is prohibited from marrying again, and she is prohibited, not having to marry except to a brother. How, therefore, will the Apostle agree with the Law, which he does not attack in its entirety, when we come to his letter, it will be shown. Meanwhile, what pertains to the Law, those arguments are more suitable for us. Finally, it prohibits the same, priests from marrying again. It also commands the daughter of a priest, if she is a widow or has been cast out, and if she does not have children, to return to her father's house and be fed from his bread. Therefore, if she does not have children, she will not marry again, not as if she had children; but so that, if she has children, she may be nourished by her son rather than by her father, so that the son may also fulfill the command of God, Honor your father and mother. But we, Jesus, the high priest and great Father, clothing us with his own, made us priests to God the Father according to John. For he also recalls that young man hastening to his father's funeral, in order to show that we are called priests by him, whom the law forbade to be present at the burial of parents: Over every dead soul the priest will not enter, and over his father and over his mother he will not be defiled. Therefore, should we also observe this interdict? Not certainly. For our one Father, God, lives, and Mother, the Church; and we are not dead, who live to God; nor do we bury the dead, because they also live in Christ. Certainly, we are priests called by Christ, debtors of monogamy from the ancient law of God, which then prophesied us in its priests.

pass_b_english: Having worked through the ancient examples of the original figures, let us now turn to the ancient instruments of the legal Scriptures, so that we may reconsider our entire preparation in proper order. Some people sometimes claim they have nothing to do with the law—which Christ did not dissolve but fulfilled—yet at other times they grab whatever parts of the law suit them. We too say plainly that the law has passed away: its burdens, which even the Fathers refused to bear according to the judgment of the Apostles, have been conceded; but what pertains to justice not only remains reserved but has actually been expanded, so that our justice may surpass that of the Scribes and Pharisees. If justice is expanded, then chastity is as well. If, therefore, the law commands a man to take his brother’s childless widow into marriage to raise up seed for his brother—and this could happen repeatedly to one man, as the Sadducees’ cunning question shows—they conclude that frequent remarriage is permitted. They ought first to understand the reason behind that command; then they will see that the reason has ceased along with the things that have been evacuated from the law. It was necessary for the brother to marry his deceased brother’s widow. First, because the old blessing still had to run its course: “Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28). Next, because the sins of the fathers were exacted from the children. Third, because eunuchs and the sterile were held in ignominy. So, lest men who died not by nature’s debt but by death’s prevention be judged accursed, a vicarious, as it were posthumous, offspring was provided for them from their own kin. But when both “Be fruitful and multiply” and the extremity of the times have been evacuated—the Apostle introducing: “It remains that those who have wives should be as if they had none, because the time is shortened” (1 Corinthians 7:29); and “The sour grape which the fathers ate will set the children’s teeth on edge”: “For each one will die in his own sin” (Ezekiel 18:2)—and eunuchs not only escaped ignominy but merited grace, invited into the kingdoms of heaven, the law of marrying a brother’s widow having been buried, its contrary—not marrying a brother’s widow—prevailed. And so, as we said before, what has ceased to be valid, its reason having ceased, cannot support another argument. Therefore the wife of a deceased husband will not marry—certainly not the brother, if she marries at all. For we are all brothers: and marriage “in the Lord” means marrying not a Gentile but a brother; because even the old law forbade marriage with foreigners. But when Leviticus also warns: “Whoever takes his brother’s wife—it is impurity, shame; he will die childless” (Leviticus 18:16)—there is no doubt that while he is prohibited from marrying again, she is prohibited too, having no one to marry except a brother. How, then, will the Apostle agree with the Law, which he does not attack in its entirety? When we come to his letter it will be shown. Meanwhile, the arguments that belong to the Law suit us better. Finally, the same Law prohibits priests from marrying again. It also commands the daughter of a priest, if she is a widow or cast out and has no children, to return to her father’s house and eat of his bread. Therefore, if she has no children, she will not marry again—not as she would if she had them; but so that, if she has children, she may be supported by her son rather than her father, that the son may also fulfill God’s command: “Honor your father and mother.’ But we, Jesus the high priest and great Father, clothing us with his own, made us priests to God his Father according to John. For he also recalls that young man hurrying to his father’s funeral, to show that we are called priests by him whom the law forbade to attend the burial of parents: “Over every dead soul the priest shall not enter, and over his father and over his mother he shall not be defiled” (Leviticus 21:1-4). Therefore should we also observe this interdict? Certainly not. For our one Father, God, lives, and our Mother, the Church; and we are not dead, who live to God; nor do we bury the dead, because they also live in Christ. Certainly we are priests called by Christ, debtors of monogamy from the ancient law of God, which then prophesied us in its priests.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A preserves the sense of all clauses, and Pass B provides the necessary scriptural identifications (Genesis 1:28, 1 Corinthians 7:29, Ezekiel 18:2, Leviticus 18:16, Leviticus 21:1-4) which were alluded to in the Latin but not explicitly numbered. The distinction between 'justice' and 'chastity' (justitia/pudicitia) is maintained. The complex argument regarding the cessation of the levirate marriage due to the change in the 'reason' (ratione) is correctly rendered.
